Harsh,

To my thinking we all get better when we try these things. I'm not any kind of eligible, and barely legible, but I'll have a crack at this.

One of the defining elements of an FTR is a liquidity gap (wide bodied candle) away from the retrace. This would mean that your move B would invalidate A as an FTR. The move away from B would need to be a LQ to show an imbalance between supply and demand, and thus a higher probability of a reaction on the return.

Ok IF, I have recently been pondering this kind of scenario, so it was already something I had planned on digging into. This seems a good time to do it. There is a lot on here and it got kinda cramped, but hopefully its still legible. I just kept finding stuff and wanted to label it. There are still a few things I left off.

In order to convey what I am thinking I used a new term. It should work till you or someone comes up with something better. STR - since price can't just keep going on forever, at some point it has to return back into the PAZ. But this is what really struck me while making this up:

1) Price breaks a high and keeps going till supply hits it and leaves a HH 2) comes back to form an FTR at the old high 3) trades back up and makes a LH 4) falls back down to the FTR, it usually reacts for at least a small move to make another LH, but can fall through the FTR. Just know you may go into DD if your in the market and price fails to make a new high/low. 5) price then returns back into the PAZ that it left at 1. It may react to pockets of demand on the way down, but it ultimately wants the demand that created the HH.

Now here is the kicker for me. If you draw a horizontal line from the high that was origanilly broke at 1, even though there are a bunch of candles now that you had to draw the line through, when price hits that demand and trades up and through the line it leaves an FTR at the line (the old high at 1). Once price fell back into the PAZ and reacted to demand, it tested the PAZ high again, even though there are a bunch of candles there this time, before continuing on the second time. I don't know how often this happens, and I need to do some more studies to make sure, but it happened 3 times on the one chart, all at HTF supply.

Hope this makes as much sense to you guys as it does me.
